mechanisms.conditioning_logic: Compute the joint pairing of (Team B corners FOR) with (Team A corners AGAINST) and separately (Team A corners FOR) with (Team B corners AGAINST), then assess whether the combined cross-team corner imbalance signal — both dimensions simultaneously — predicts corner totals and corner winner beyond what either team's own mirror alone captures.
mechanisms.expected_relationship_to_test: Matches where one team's FOR corners and the opponent's AGAINST corners are both extreme in the same direction (large imbalance on both dimensions simultaneously) should show a stronger skew in corner distribution toward the dominant team than matches where only one dimension is extreme.
mechanisms.mechanism_statement: Team B's corner-kick dominance (high FOR, low AGAINST) interacts jointly with Team A's corner-kick deficit (low FOR, high AGAINST) to produce an asymmetric corner-kick imbalance that is structurally different from either team's single-observable mirror. The joint cross-team corner differential — Team B's FOR minus Team A's FOR, and Team A's AGAINST minus Team B's AGAINST — should be measured together as a two-observable, two-team joint signal.
mechanisms.why_not_baseline_equivalent: The engine covers each team's own FOR vs opponent's AGAINST as a same-observable mirror independently. This mechanism requires the joint evaluation of both teams' FOR and AGAINST corner rates simultaneously — a two-team, two-perspective joint relationship — which is not reducible to a single observable with one conditioning band.

mechanisms.conditioning_logic: Split corner production by half for both teams. Condition on whether Team B's first-half corner FOR rate substantially exceeds its second-half rate, and whether Team A's first-half corner AGAINST rate differs from its second-half AGAINST rate, to test whether the half-level imbalance is consistent or reverses across halves.
mechanisms.expected_relationship_to_test: When Team B's first-half corner FOR rate is disproportionately higher than its second-half rate, and Team A's first-half corner AGAINST rate is also elevated, the first half should show a stronger corner skew toward Team B than the second half — i.e., the within-match half distribution of corners is non-uniform and directionally predictable.
mechanisms.mechanism_statement: Team B's corner-kick production is heavily front-loaded into the first half (FOR first-half mean notably higher than second-half mean), while Team A concedes corners more evenly across halves. The joint within-match half-level distribution of corners — Team B's first-half corner FOR rate relative to its second-half rate, conditioned on Team A's half-level AGAINST rates — should be measured as a within-match state mechanism.
mechanisms.why_not_baseline_equivalent: This requires a within-match half-level split of a single observable conditioned on both teams' half-level rates simultaneously — a within-match state dependence combining two teams' half-period observables. It is not a simple recent vs. long-run comparison or a single coarse band split.

mechanisms.conditioning_logic: Jointly condition on (a) the possession gap between the two teams being large (Team B FOR possession far above competition context mean of 50%) and (b) Team A's shots-on-target FOR rate relative to its shots FOR rate (on-target conversion ratio). Test whether the combination of extreme possession asymmetry and low shot quality for the possession-deficit team produces a suppression of goals FOR for Team A beyond what either observable alone predicts.
mechanisms.expected_relationship_to_test: When possession asymmetry is large and the lower-possession team's shot-on-target ratio is also below the competition mean, goals FOR for the lower-possession team should be further suppressed relative to matches where only one of these conditions holds.
mechanisms.mechanism_statement: Team B's high possession dominance (FOR ~69%) is jointly paired with Team A's low shot conversion efficiency (high shots AGAINST, low goals FOR relative to shots FOR). The relationship between Team B's possession advantage and Team A's shots-to-goals conversion ratio should be measured as a joint two-observable signal: whether extreme possession asymmetry co-occurs with suppressed shot quality for the lower-possession team (Team A), producing a non-linear interaction between possession share and shot conversion.
mechanisms.why_not_baseline_equivalent: This is a genuine joint relationship between two distinct observables (possession and shot quality ratio) for two different teams simultaneously. It cannot be reduced to a single observable mirror or a single coarse band split — it requires the interaction of possession asymmetry with shot conversion efficiency across teams.

mechanisms.conditioning_logic: Jointly condition on Team B's first-half goals FOR rate and Team A's second-half goals AGAINST rate. Test whether matches where Team B has a high first-half scoring rate AND Team A has a high second-half conceding rate produce a specific within-match goal timing pattern (goals concentrated in both halves but for different structural reasons) that differs from the competition context baseline.
mechanisms.expected_relationship_to_test: When Team B's first-half goals FOR rate is elevated above competition context and Team A's second-half goals AGAINST rate is also elevated, the within-match goal distribution should show a non-uniform half-level pattern — with Team B goals skewed earlier and Team A concessions skewed later — rather than the uniform distribution implied by treating each half independently.
mechanisms.mechanism_statement: Team B's goals are heavily skewed toward the first half (FOR first-half mean ~1.21 vs second-half ~1.46 across 80 matches, but first-half rate is notably high relative to competition context goals mean of ~1.47 per match total), while Team A concedes more in the second half than the first half. The asymmetric within-match half-level goal distribution — Team B scoring more in the first half while Team A concedes more in the second half — should be measured as a joint cross-team half-level goal timing mechanism.
mechanisms.why_not_baseline_equivalent: This requires jointly conditioning on two teams' half-level goal rates simultaneously (Team B first-half FOR and Team A second-half AGAINST), which is a within-match state dependence across two distinct half-period observables for two teams. It is not reducible to a single observable with one coarse band.

mechanisms.conditioning_logic: Jointly condition on (a) Team A's recent-5 foul FOR rate being substantially below its all-prior rate AND (b) Team B's recent-5 foul FOR rate being substantially below its all-prior rate. Test whether this joint foul-rate regime shift (both teams trending lower simultaneously) is associated with suppressed second-half card volume relative to the competition context cards_2h baseline.
mechanisms.expected_relationship_to_test: When both teams show a concurrent downward regime shift in foul rates (recent trend below long-run baseline for both), second-half card volume should be suppressed relative to the competition context mean — and this suppression should be stronger than when only one team shows a foul-rate decline.
mechanisms.mechanism_statement: Team A's foul rate has declined sharply in recent matches (FOR recent-5 mean ~9.2 vs all-prior ~12.0), while Team B's foul rate has also declined (FOR recent-5 ~8.6 vs all-prior ~9.5). The joint recent-trend trajectory of both teams' foul rates — both declining simultaneously — should be measured against the second-half cards rate (cards_2h), to test whether a joint foul-rate regime shift for both teams co-occurs with a suppression of second-half card volume relative to the competition context baseline.
mechanisms.why_not_baseline_equivalent: This mechanism requires jointly conditioning on two teams' recent-vs-long-run foul rate trajectories simultaneously, then linking that joint regime shift to a different observable (cards_2h). It combines a sequencing/regime structure (recent vs. all-prior) for two teams with a cross-observable relationship (fouls to cards), which is not reducible to any single observable with one conditioning band.
